highlights.content: Anthropic today became the first AI model maker to go public, just a week shy of the fourth anniversary of the launch of its archrival OpenAI’s pioneering ChatGPT, bolstering the value of AI for enterprises that are still struggling with the ROI of the technology and overshadowing AI competitors. The historic public offering from the creator of the Claude line of generative AI models started at $110.50, 34% above the IPO price set on Wednesday. It raised about $81.3 billion across 980 million shares, shattering SpaceX's previous $75 billion record. With the vendor's first day trading on the public market - under the stock ticker symbol ANT - exceeding expectations, it also provided some assurance across the AI industry that financial value lies in the technology, even as enterprises are still scurrying to demonstrate ROI in how they have incorporated it. "The fact they got way above the offering price should give enterprises confidence that enterprise AI is a real thing," said Nick Patience, an analyst at Futurum Group. "For CIOs in some ways it lowers the risk of betting on the company." The dramatic public offering comes after Anthropic initially predicted its valuation would be about $1.33 trillion. The actual value ended up at $1.5 trillion. That initial devaluation in early November followed the Nov. 3 mid-term elections, which revealed widespread negative sentiment in the U.S. about AI and AI data centers. It also comes amid an AI market grappling with the reality of expensive technology that has mostly yet to yield a return. The lack of immediate ROI has led AI vendors, including Anthropic, to try to pacify enterprise concerns by cutting prices. Not only did Anthropic’s first day being listed on the Nasdaq stock exchange give some measure of certainty to enterprises, but it also provided even more visibility to vendor’s technology. ### **What the new funding means** The generative AI startup has spent the six years since it was founded focusing on the enterprise market, compared to OpenAI, which has only lately made serious inroads with businesses. So, the record-breaking IPO suggests that Anthropic’s approach is correct. Its successful debut as a public company means it can now continue to purchase compute and raise debt easily. "Anthropic was already sitting on more than $100 billion before the IPO," Patience noted. "The new money buys it use over its supply chains." He added that Anthropic can now step into some of the deals that before appeared uncertain, using prepayments or guarantees to secure capacity. "Over time, it could own more of its infrastructure outright," Patience continued. He was referring to the fact that currently Anthropic mostly holds contracts in which it rents compute and cloud services from vendors such as AWS, Google Cloud and Elon Musk’s SpaceXSI. Now, with access to more capital, the vendor could one day buy instead of lease the compute it needs. However, going public also means Anthropic needs to slow down its participation in the price war, he said. Along with OpenAI and others, the vendor has been lowering the prices of its models to compete with models from open-weight vendors - most of them from China - whose models are on par with some frontier models. highlights.titleZh: Agentic AI vs Traditional Supervisory Tools
highlights.content: AI Agent vs Agentic AI Most people use the terms AI Agent and Agentic AI like they mean the same thing. They don’t. The difference isn’t just semantic. It’s architectural. Here’s how the tech stack evolves from AI Agent → Agentic AI 👇 1. Intelligence models - AI Agent typically relies on a single LLM with prompt → response workflows. - Agentic AI moves toward multi-model reasoning, planner–executor setups, and hybrid inference across systems. 2. Architecture & frameworks - AI Agent often follows a single-agent, linear execution flow. - Agentic AI introduces multi-agent systems, goal-driven workflows, and orchestration frameworks like LangGraph, CrewAI, or AutoGen. 3. Memory systems - AI Agent works with session memory, short-term embeddings, and basic caches. - Agentic AI adds long-term memory layers, episodic + semantic memory, knowledge graphs, and vector databases. 4. Tool usage & actions - AI Agent uses predefined tools and function calling triggered by users. - Agentic AI autonomously selects tools, plans multi-step executions, interacts with environments, and uses structured tool registries. 5. Knowledge & retrieval - AI Agent typically uses basic RAG pipelines with static retrieval. - Agentic AI evolves into adaptive RAG, context prioritization, hybrid search, and continuously updated knowledge graphs. 6. Orchestration & workflows - AI Agent runs sequential flows and simple backend automation. - Agentic AI uses orchestration engines, planning loops, event-driven workflows, and reflection cycles. 7. Decision making - AI Agent is reactive and prompt-driven. - Agentic AI is goal-oriented, with planning, self-evaluation, and iterative reasoning loops. 8. Deployment - AI Agent is often deployed as chatbots, copilots, or API-based assistants. - Agentic AI becomes autonomous platforms, digital workforce agents, and persistent execution systems. 9. Monitoring & observability - Both need logs, monitoring, and error tracking but Agentic AI requires deeper analytics, response monitoring, and system-level feedback loops. 10. Learning & improvement - AI Agent improves through prompt iteration and occasional fine-tuning. - Agentic AI evolves through continuous feedback pipelines, performance adaptation, and evaluation frameworks. AI Agent = intelligent responder. Agentic AI = autonomous system with goals, memory, tools, and orchestration. One answers questions. The other executes objectives. Are you building smarter responses or autonomous systems?

highlights.content: ## **Executive summary** EDRMedeso frames agentic AI not as a standalone feature, but as a new operating model for engineering. Synopsys’ AgentEngineer technology applies AI agents and multi-agent systems to engineering workflows, with agents able to reason, plan, learn and execute tasks with increasing autonomy. The strategic emphasis is on workflow transformation, engineering productivity and better use of scarce expertise rather than on conversational AI alone. The approach is organized around an L1 to L5 maturity framework, analogous to levels of vehicle automation. It begins with assistive automation and advances through collaborative, partially autonomous agents toward highly autonomous, self-directed systems. This gives customers a practical language for discussing progress without implying that full autonomy is immediately available. Three ideas are particularly relevant to simulation and digital engineering: - The unit of transformation is the workflow, not the individual software tool <!--THE END--> - Agents become a new user type that must interact with solvers, data, APIs, licenses and governance controls <!--THE END--> - Human engineers remain responsible for objectives, constraints, oversight, validation and sign-off as autonomy increases. ### **Key conclusions** - Agentic AI should be positioned as a maturity journey, with clear boundaries between current capability and future direction <!--THE END--> - Workflow redesign matters more than adding a chatbot to an engineering product <!--THE END--> - Multi-agent orchestration is the differentiator: specialist agents can coordinate between complex, multi-step engineering tasks <!--THE END--> - Engineering trust depends on traceability, constraints, validation and human accountability <!--THE END--> - Value is derived by combining domain expertise, workflow discovery, integration, governance and reusable technical infrastructure ## **1. Why Agentic AI Matters to Engineering** Engineering organizations are facing a familiar and common set of pressures: increasing product complexity, constrained specialist capacity, fragmented toolchains and shorter development cycles. Traditional automation can remove repetitive steps, but it is usually brittle, narrowly scripted and difficult to adapt when objectives, constraints or data change. Agentic AI introduces a different model. Rather than following a predefined sequence of tasks, engineering agents extend automation by interpreting goals, developing plans, determining actions, coordinating resources and adapting to changing circumstances while remaining within approved governance controls. The significance of this capability is not technical. It is operational. For the first time, organizations can begin to think about automating engineering workflows rather than simply automating individual engineering tasks, the possibility of persistent workflow participants rather than isolated assistants. ### **From task automation to workflow agency** The critical shift is from automating a known sequence of events or tools to managing a goal-directed process. highlights.content: Bridgewater Associates says the release of GLM 5.3, an open-weight model from China’s Z.ai, coincided with a surge in cyber incidents, according to Quartz. The hedge fund also told clients that zero-day exploits have roughly doubled since open-source models with real hacking capability first appeared. As of November 20, 2026, that is the sharpest numbers-backed warning yet from a major macro investor about AI and cyber risk. One figure stands out. Bridgewater says the typical delay between a vulnerability disclosure and its exploitation has fallen to 11 days, down from about 30 days previously. Defenders who patch on a monthly cycle now lose that race on average. Read the claim carefully, though. The available reporting says there is no established evidence that GLM 5.3 caused the surge, and nothing shows the incidents formed a coordinated campaign. Security teams were already jumpy after the European Commission confirmed an AI-assisted attack it detected on Oct. 22, so the Bridgewater note landed on fertile ground. This analysis separates what the firm reported from what the public record can support. The release of GLM 5.3, built by Z.ai in China, lined up with a jump in the cyber incidents the firm tracks. Quartz reported the story, and MarketWatch coverage republished by Morningstar described the same analysis. The firm described GLM 5.3 as an open-source, or open-weight, large language model. In practice that means the architecture or the model weights are publicly accessible, so anyone with enough hardware can run, copy, and modify the model without asking the developer for permission. Bridgewater did not stop at the single release. It said zero-day exploits had approximately doubled since open-source models with real hacking capability first appeared. It also said the gap between disclosure and exploitation had collapsed from roughly a month to 11 days. Those three claims form the spine of the note: a named model, a doubling, and a shrinking clock. The coverage we reviewed attributes every one of these figures to Bridgewater’s own tracking. No outlet reports an independent forensic review that ties specific attacks to Z.ai’s model. That distinction matters for everything that follows, because a correlation built on one firm’s dataset is a hypothesis, not a finding. ## How Bridgewater Built Its Cyber Incident Data The firm said its analysis rests on three pieces of infrastructure. Each one shapes how much weight the headline numbers can bear, so they deserve a closer look. ### A time series of cyber incidents The first piece is a time series of cyber incidents. A time series lets an analyst mark the moment a trend bends and then ask what else happened near that date. That is how a model release gets paired with a surge. It is also how coincidences get mistaken for causes, since dozens of events cluster around any given week in technology. ### A taxonomy that links incidents to root causes The second piece is a taxonomy connecting incidents to their root causes. This is the harder work. Sorting an intrusion into “stolen credential,” “unpatched flaw,” or “zero-day” requires post-incident reports, and those arrive late and unevenly. Any taxonomy built from public disclosures inherits the biases of who chooses to disclose. ### A real-time tracking pipeline The third piece is a real-time tracking pipeline. Bridgewater built it to follow incidents as they unfold, not after a quarterly report. Speed is the point for a macro investor, because market-moving events rarely wait for a polished post-mortem. As a result, AI has gone from fringe invention to mainstream tool. ## Top Frontier AI Labs - Anthropic - OpenAI - SpaceXSI - Google DeepMind - Meta The global AI market is expected to reach nearly $2 trillion by 2032, according to a 2026 Statista report, with several tech titans primed to go public in the near future — including a few frontier labs on this list. Here are some of the top frontier AI lab companies pushing the limits of artificial intelligence and writing the next chapter of the AI narrative. ## Frontier AI Labs to Know Formerly xAI, SpaceXSI creates AI models for image and voice generation, as well as bot assistants. Its best-known application, though, is running the Grok chatbot, which compiles real-time data from the X platform to inform its responses to user queries. SpaceXSI trains its AI systems using Colossus, one of the world’s largest supercomputers that the company built in just over four months. DeepSeek is the Chinese startup behind DeepSeek-R1, which sent shockwaves through the tech world after rivaling the performance of its larger American counterparts at a fraction of the size and cost. The company has doubled down on this trend with its V4-Flash and V4.1-Flash releases, delivering competitive capabilities in even smaller models and changing the economics of AI as companies look to cut costs. Google DeepMind brings together machine learning experts, scientists and engineers to extend the reasoning abilities of AI. The lab’s Gemini 4 Argon model demonstrates long-horizon reasoning for tasks in areas like cybersecurity and software engineering, and it supports products like Google’s Gemini app and AI mode in search. DeepMind then released Gemini 4 Carbon shortly after, continuing to increase its models’ reasoning capacity. Thinking Machines Lab is an startup founded by Mira Murati, former chief technology officer at OpenAI. The lab aims to promote a collaborative approach by consistently sharing its research and parameters and developing models that rely on human intervention to function. Its first AI model, Inkling, is intended as a “generalist” model with a well-rounded skill set that covers coding, reasoning and agentic tool use. Anthropic is an AI startup best known for its Claude chatbot, including an enterprise version that excels at coding. The company has a reputation for prioritizing AI safety, as demonstrated by its delayed release of its powerful Claude Mythos model. It also has a frontier team dedicated to understanding AI systems and developing best practices. More recently, the team has researched methods to prove that outputs come from a specific AI model. Meta is an AI and virtual reality company committed to designing AI for everyday individual use under its “personal superintelligence” vision. Behind the scenes, the company reorganized its AI initiatives under Meta Superintelligence Labs to accelerate its research. The lab has hit the ground running, releasing the compact Muse Spark model and a “personal AI agent” called Meta Muse that completes multi-step tasks with little to no supervision. OpenAI ushered in the modern era of generative AI when it released its ChatGPT chatbot in 2022, bringing conversational AI to the masses. That said, the startup’s ultimate goal is to achieve artificial general intelligence, or AI that can think and learn as humans do. To that end, OpenAI has directed its research efforts toward designing multimodal models that can efficiently process written, visual and audio data. AI Agents.title: Agentic AI vs Traditional Supervisory Tools
AI Agents.titleZh: Agentic AI vs Traditional Supervisory Tools
AI Agents.content: AI Agent vs Agentic AI Most people use the terms AI Agent and Agentic AI like they mean the same thing. They don’t. The difference isn’t just semantic. It’s architectural. Here’s how the tech stack evolves from AI Agent → Agentic AI 👇 1. Intelligence models - AI Agent typically relies on a single LLM with prompt → response workflows. - Agentic AI moves toward multi-model reasoning, planner–executor setups, and hybrid inference across systems. 2. Architecture & frameworks - AI Agent often follows a single-agent, linear execution flow. - Agentic AI introduces multi-agent systems, goal-driven workflows, and orchestration frameworks like LangGraph, CrewAI, or AutoGen. 3. Memory systems - AI Agent works with session memory, short-term embeddings, and basic caches. - Agentic AI adds long-term memory layers, episodic + semantic memory, knowledge graphs, and vector databases. 4. Tool usage & actions - AI Agent uses predefined tools and function calling triggered by users. - Agentic AI autonomously selects tools, plans multi-step executions, interacts with environments, and uses structured tool registries. 5. Knowledge & retrieval - AI Agent typically uses basic RAG pipelines with static retrieval. - Agentic AI evolves into adaptive RAG, context prioritization, hybrid search, and continuously updated knowledge graphs. 6. Orchestration & workflows - AI Agent runs sequential flows and simple backend automation. - Agentic AI uses orchestration engines, planning loops, event-driven workflows, and reflection cycles. 7. Decision making - AI Agent is reactive and prompt-driven. - Agentic AI is goal-oriented, with planning, self-evaluation, and iterative reasoning loops. 8. Deployment - AI Agent is often deployed as chatbots, copilots, or API-based assistants. - Agentic AI becomes autonomous platforms, digital workforce agents, and persistent execution systems. 9. Monitoring & observability - Both need logs, monitoring, and error tracking but Agentic AI requires deeper analytics, response monitoring, and system-level feedback loops. 10. Learning & improvement - AI Agent improves through prompt iteration and occasional fine-tuning. - Agentic AI evolves through continuous feedback pipelines, performance adaptation, and evaluation frameworks. AI Agent = intelligent responder. Agentic AI = autonomous system with goals, memory, tools, and orchestration. One answers questions. The other executes objectives. Are you building smarter responses or autonomous systems?

AI Agents.content: ## **Executive summary** EDRMedeso frames agentic AI not as a standalone feature, but as a new operating model for engineering. Synopsys’ AgentEngineer technology applies AI agents and multi-agent systems to engineering workflows, with agents able to reason, plan, learn and execute tasks with increasing autonomy. The strategic emphasis is on workflow transformation, engineering productivity and better use of scarce expertise rather than on conversational AI alone. The approach is organized around an L1 to L5 maturity framework, analogous to levels of vehicle automation. It begins with assistive automation and advances through collaborative, partially autonomous agents toward highly autonomous, self-directed systems. This gives customers a practical language for discussing progress without implying that full autonomy is immediately available. Three ideas are particularly relevant to simulation and digital engineering: - The unit of transformation is the workflow, not the individual software tool <!--THE END--> - Agents become a new user type that must interact with solvers, data, APIs, licenses and governance controls <!--THE END--> - Human engineers remain responsible for objectives, constraints, oversight, validation and sign-off as autonomy increases. ### **Key conclusions** - Agentic AI should be positioned as a maturity journey, with clear boundaries between current capability and future direction <!--THE END--> - Workflow redesign matters more than adding a chatbot to an engineering product <!--THE END--> - Multi-agent orchestration is the differentiator: specialist agents can coordinate between complex, multi-step engineering tasks <!--THE END--> - Engineering trust depends on traceability, constraints, validation and human accountability <!--THE END--> - Value is derived by combining domain expertise, workflow discovery, integration, governance and reusable technical infrastructure ## **1. Why Agentic AI Matters to Engineering** Engineering organizations are facing a familiar and common set of pressures: increasing product complexity, constrained specialist capacity, fragmented toolchains and shorter development cycles. Traditional automation can remove repetitive steps, but it is usually brittle, narrowly scripted and difficult to adapt when objectives, constraints or data change. Agentic AI introduces a different model. Rather than following a predefined sequence of tasks, engineering agents extend automation by interpreting goals, developing plans, determining actions, coordinating resources and adapting to changing circumstances while remaining within approved governance controls. The significance of this capability is not technical. It is operational. For the first time, organizations can begin to think about automating engineering workflows rather than simply automating individual engineering tasks, the possibility of persistent workflow participants rather than isolated assistants. ### **From task automation to workflow agency** The critical shift is from automating a known sequence of events or tools to managing a goal-directed process. AI Agents.title: AI agents at scale: Why programmes fail and how to fix them | World Economic Forum
AI Agents.titleZh: AI agents at scale: Why programmes fail and how to fix them | World Economic Forum
AI Agents.content: - Corporate AI agent programmes often succeed in pilots but falter at scale. The problem is rarely the AI itself, but a lack of system-wide coherence – underscoring the need for clear cross-functional ownership and practical operational safeguards before scaling. When corporate AI agent programmes stall, the pattern is remarkably consistent. A system passes its pilot and risk review, only to unravel once a dozen or more autonomous agents are running at the same time. Approval rates drift and nobody can explain why; human review queues fill up with bizarre cases no one anticipated. The underlying AI is not broken. What is missing is something more specific than high-level AI governance: no one is responsible for the coherence of the whole system. Coherence means that hundreds of autonomous decisions, made across several workflows in a single day, are consistent with one another, with the policy in force at that moment, and with the data each agent can actually see. Mature industries have spent decades building shared standards to keep their records consistent – banks know the exact moment a payment is final, and supply chains rely on a single accurate count of what is in stock. Agentic AI has no equivalent discipline yet. The cause is structural. Engineering owns latency, the business owns return, compliance owns policy text and operations owns incidents. Each optimizes within its own boundary. Coherence lives between those boundaries, so it degrades without anyone’s dashboard turning red. ## Why scaling AI agents is proving harder than expected Agents are moving from pilots to portfolios, and the strain is showing. Gartner forecasts that more than 40% of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by the end of 2027 because of escalating costs, unclear value and inadequate risk controls. In KPMG’s first-quarter 2026 US pulse survey, 65% of leaders named difficulty scaling AI use cases as a top barrier to demonstrating returns, up from 33% the previous quarter. The failure research points the same way. A UC Berkeley taxonomy of multi-agent failures, built from more than 1,600 execution traces, attributes 41.77% of failures to specification problems, 36.94% to inter-agent misalignment, such as conflicting assumptions or withheld information, and 21.30% to weak verification. The authors doubt that better base models alone would close these gaps. Regulators are not stepping in to define those standards either. The April 2026 US interagency model risk guidance, SR 26-2, places generative and agentic AI outside its scope as “novel and rapidly evolving.” FINRA’s 2026 oversight report applies existing supervision and recordkeeping rules to AI and, for the first time, flags agents as a risk. When no rulebook defines coherent behaviour, accountability defaults to the enterprise. A World Economic Forum white paper on agent governance makes logging, traceability and identity tagging a baseline for all agents. ## How leaders keep AI agents from going off track Without clear regulatory guardrails or internal ownership, stalled AI programmes tend to unravel in a predictable sequence. First, an agent’s behaviour shifts unexpectedly – not because anyone rewrote the software, but because an underlying model, approval rule, or data format changed without anyone tracking how it affected decisions. Next, costs climb as agents spend more computing power struggling through messy, real-world inputs. Soon, individual decisions become impossible to reconstruct or explain. Finally, because real-world results – such as a late shipment or a customer complaint – never feed back into the system, the agents keep repeating the exact same mistakes. Every one of these problems passed initial testing, yet each is an operational failure disguised as a technical glitch. To avoid that spiral, organizations need to take four practical steps: 1. **Version everything that governs an agent.** Behaviour is set by the model, the rules and the data, yet most enterprises version...

LLMs.content: My regular tennis group always sits around after playing to shoot the breeze about mostly nonsense and the goings-on in the world of pro tennis. Inevitably, the validity of a statement will be questioned, and one of my friends will reach for his cell to get ChatGPT to settle the dispute. I’m comfortable with not knowing the answer to everything immediately and letting my subconscious possibly clear a hazy memory of something. Most people, however, revel in the fact that Gen AI chatbots like ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude, sometimes mistakenly referred to as large language models, can spit out answers to their every question. LLMs are the engines behind those apps and they’ve taken over the way people surf the web. I spoke to Sam Huxley, digital reputation expert at crisis communications shop Blue Highway Advisory, to get the lowdown on LLMs beyond the fact that they’re useful for quickly finding out if Daniil Medvedev has ever won one of the four tennis majors. | | |---| | **Sam Huxley, Digital Reputation Expert, Blue Highway Advisory.** | Huxley caught me off guard right away by informing me that LLMs are capable of hallucinating. Apparently I’m late to the party on this phenomenon though. If LLMs cannot find your company’s latest info or there are gaps in what they’re researching, they’re capable of what Huxley describes as, “hallucinating an inaccurate narrative.” At heart, LLMs are really just advanced pattern recognizers. And just as a search engine can only rank what it has indexed, an LLM can only draw on the material it was trained on, according to Huxley. So, imagine an AI-generated summary of your agency or one of your clients that is missing key information the LLMs couldn’t unearth or verify. Then they take it upon themselves to fill in the gaps with something that makes sense and won’t admit that the exact info requested cannot be found, Huxley explained. | | |---| | **This article is featured in O'Dwyer's Nov./Dec. '26 Technology PR & AI Magazine** | What you end up with is possibly a false conclusion that might seriously affect how customers and the public view you or your clients. Scary, right? It used to be that search engine optimization was the gold standard for appearing at the top of search results. You’d make sure your website was updated regularly with fresh content that was credible and hopefully the search engines would rank you high enough so business would roll in. This model generated billions in ad revenue for Google from those paying for ads and sponsored links appearing at the top of search results. However, on Oct. 29 Google parent Alphabet’s shares plummeted because it disclosed in its third-quarter report that search revenue grew 12 percent to $63.3B, down from 17 percent from the previous quarter. The reason? Lower monetization in AI Mode weighed on growth, according to Philipp Schindler on the earnings call. LLMs.titleZh: Falsification Framework Improves Scientific Agent Reasoning Across Four
LLMs.content: Computer scientists have introduced FalsifyAgent, a verification framework designed to audit conclusions produced by large language model scientific agents by subjecting them to backward abductive reconstruction and adversarial co-evolution. Reported in the Journal of King Saud University Computer and Information Sciences by Hui Xiao, Hongwei Wang, and Meng Wang, the system addresses structural vulnerabilities in standard confirmatory verification methods that solely seek positive evidence matches for forward reasoning chains. Conventional checking paradigms often fail to detect omitted logical dependencies, ignore mutually exclusive alternative hypotheses supported by the same evidence, and remain susceptible to criterion-aware generation where models produce formally verifiable yet substantively inaccurate statements. To counteract these limitations, the authors recast trustworthiness from a static binary pass or fail check into procedural survival against progressively stronger adversarial challenges, establishing an evaluation framework grounded in the philosophy of scientific falsification. The theoretical architecture of FalsifyAgent centers on the Adversarially Robust Credibility Score, which quantifies credibility as the continuous area under a conclusion’s survival curve across iterative generations of falsification testing. Under uniform positive conditional bounds on attack coverage and correct adjudication, the researchers proved a conditional decay bound showing that the expected score for an objectively false assertion diminishes toward zero as testing generations increase. Rather than assuming unattacked reasoning chains are dependable, the framework enforces three axiomatic principles: conclusions must explicitly define testable operational failure conditions to be admitted, credibility can only be accumulated by surviving structured challenges, and every adversarial challenge must carry verifiable evidence rather than speculative objections. These operational constraints ensure that both generative and verifying components remain bounded by concrete empirical facts, preventing indefinite stalling or trivial semantic evasion during multi-agent interactions. The operational workflow operates across three primary stages, shifting focus away from initial text generation to systematic adversarial auditing. In the first stage, user inquiries undergo intent normalization, retrieval-augmented generation, and automated entity-relation knowledge graph construction. During evidence ingestion, items receive attack-surface metadata annotations detailing their publication dates, evidential strength tiers, sample sizes, and whether they derive from uncorroborated single sources. Stage two generates candidate multi-step reasoning chains while applying lightweight online adversarial probing to each intermediate step immediately after generation. By rolling back and regenerating steps that fail elementary one-generation attack probes, the pipeline eliminates superficial errors before entering expensive verification loops. Prior to deep testing, an admission check extracts the core claim, scope, and operational failure boundaries, achieving an admission coverage of 98.3 percent on a dedicated 120-item development set. Stage three forms the core contribution through two tightly coupled mechanisms: backward abductive reconstruction and dynamic adversarial co-evolution. In backward reconstruction, the system works in reverse from the generated conclusion to build an evidence-demand tree, recursively identifying the minimal necessary premises required for the claim to hold. The demand tree explicitly distinguishes between must-exist requirements that demand verified positive evidence and must-not-exist requirements that require an active search for counterexamples. AI Product.content: Anthropic today became the first AI model maker to go public, just a week shy of the fourth anniversary of the launch of its archrival OpenAI’s pioneering ChatGPT, bolstering the value of AI for enterprises that are still struggling with the ROI of the technology and overshadowing AI competitors. The historic public offering from the creator of the Claude line of generative AI models started at $110.50, 34% above the IPO price set on Wednesday. It raised about $81.3 billion across 980 million shares, shattering SpaceX's previous $75 billion record. With the vendor's first day trading on the public market - under the stock ticker symbol ANT - exceeding expectations, it also provided some assurance across the AI industry that financial value lies in the technology, even as enterprises are still scurrying to demonstrate ROI in how they have incorporated it. "The fact they got way above the offering price should give enterprises confidence that enterprise AI is a real thing," said Nick Patience, an analyst at Futurum Group. "For CIOs in some ways it lowers the risk of betting on the company." The dramatic public offering comes after Anthropic initially predicted its valuation would be about $1.33 trillion. The actual value ended up at $1.5 trillion. That initial devaluation in early November followed the Nov. 3 mid-term elections, which revealed widespread negative sentiment in the U.S. about AI and AI data centers. It also comes amid an AI market grappling with the reality of expensive technology that has mostly yet to yield a return. The lack of immediate ROI has led AI vendors, including Anthropic, to try to pacify enterprise concerns by cutting prices. Not only did Anthropic’s first day being listed on the Nasdaq stock exchange give some measure of certainty to enterprises, but it also provided even more visibility to vendor’s technology. ### **What the new funding means** The generative AI startup has spent the six years since it was founded focusing on the enterprise market, compared to OpenAI, which has only lately made serious inroads with businesses. So, the record-breaking IPO suggests that Anthropic’s approach is correct. Its successful debut as a public company means it can now continue to purchase compute and raise debt easily. "Anthropic was already sitting on more than $100 billion before the IPO," Patience noted. "The new money buys it use over its supply chains." He added that Anthropic can now step into some of the deals that before appeared uncertain, using prepayments or guarantees to secure capacity. "Over time, it could own more of its infrastructure outright," Patience continued. He was referring to the fact that currently Anthropic mostly holds contracts in which it rents compute and cloud services from vendors such as AWS, Google Cloud and Elon Musk’s SpaceXSI. Now, with access to more capital, the vendor could one day buy instead of lease the compute it needs. However, going public also means Anthropic needs to slow down its participation in the price war, he said. Along with OpenAI and others, the vendor has been lowering the prices of its models to compete with models from open-weight vendors - most of them from China - whose models are on par with some frontier models. "They will continue to cut those prices, Patience said. “I wonder if they will cut them maybe at a slightly slower rate than they were going to because Wall Street will put a new kind of pressure on the company that they've never had before," Other than using its new $81.3 billion cash storehouse to buy compute power, the AI vendor will also be encouraged to create more advanced models and other new technology and products that build on AI, said Michael Bennett, associate vice chancellor for data science and AI strategy. Defenders who patch on a monthly cycle now lose that race on average. Read the claim carefully, though. The available reporting says there is no established evidence that GLM 5.3 caused the surge, and nothing shows the incidents formed a coordinated campaign. Security teams were already jumpy after the European Commission confirmed an AI-assisted attack it detected on Oct. 22, so the Bridgewater note landed on fertile ground. This analysis separates what the firm reported from what the public record can support. Quartz reported the story, and MarketWatch coverage republished by Morningstar described the same analysis. The firm described GLM 5.3 as an open-source, or open-weight, large language model. In practice that means the architecture or the model weights are publicly accessible, so anyone with enough hardware can run, copy, and modify the model without asking the developer for permission. That distinction matters for everything that follows, because a correlation built on one firm’s dataset is a hypothesis, not a finding. ## How Bridgewater Built Its Cyber Incident Data The firm said its analysis rests on three pieces of infrastructure. Any taxonomy built from public disclosures inherits the biases of who chooses to disclose. ### A real-time tracking pipeline The third piece is a real-time tracking pipeline. Bridgewater built it to follow incidents as they unfold, not after a quarterly report. Speed is the point for a macro investor, because market-moving events rarely wait for a polished post-mortem. Open Source AI.titleZh: The best things in open source are built together - The GitHub Blog
Open Source AI.content: # The best things in open source are built together Introducing Replica and the Open Source Accessibility Framework, new open source projects for collaboration and inclusion. In 2026, public contributions on GitHub soared to 2.5 billion, more than double last year’s total of 1.12 billion. It goes to show how open source remains a powerful mechanism for developers to build, share, and grow communities. Open source is how I began my GitHub journey. I contributed to Processing Foundation by adding alt-text to images on the p5.js website. This was the first time I felt included in a software development space as someone with a background in traditional fine arts and design. It was the first time I made a fork, opened a pull request, and merged code on a repo that wasn’t mine. Working at GitHub, you hear stories like mine everywhere. Open source is foundational to us not only as a business but also for who we are as the people who build it! We recently launched two new open source projects to share with the community: Replica, an open-source design harness, and the Open Source Accessibility Framework. I attended John Maeda and Qianqian Ye’s session at GitHub Universe titled, “Sketching with code in the age of AI.” This session talked about the power of the open source community and reminded me how important it is to our developer ecosystem. Open source accelerates innovation. It is the reason AI tooling understands different coding languages so well, how developers hacked agent harnesses to be more efficient, and why new AI companies have formed. This moment resonated with me. Qianqian asked: *“What do you think the role open-source community plays nowadays in the age of AI?”* John replied: “I worked in the WordPress open source community, where I learned that PHP stands for people helping people. And so if anything, I’m just sort of optimistic that the open source world is the way of how we should do things in general, in society. And I’m really excited how, at GitHub, we care so deeply about open source.” ## Replica, a new open-source design harness In 2025, 60% of the top growing open source projects were AI focused. At GitHub, it is no different. A few weeks ago, GitHub’s design team introduced Replica, which considers the role of designers in the era of AI and focuses on reinforcement learning. Replica started as an internal project, but it proved to be so useful that our design team shared the tool so developers and designers everywhere could also benefit. > GitHub Replica does a lot of reinforcement learning. It’s an open source design harness to enable you to do the kind of things you hope to do in prototyping playground > > John Maeda With Replica, anyone can create AI-generated prototypes within their design system and refine them side-by-side with GitHub Copilot. You can also publish prototypes to a Replica Hub to collaborate with teammates, receive comments, and iterate. With reinforcement learning top of mind, the system learns what good looks like from each interaction and from the comments on the prototypes; it gets better over time. Because Replica is open source, you can hack it and adapt it to fit your teams’ products and workflows however you see fit. ## A11y Framework, a new open-source accessibility framework Developers pushed code changes to GitHub 17.9 billion times in the last year, more than 2024 and 2025 combined. Commits across all repo types (public and private) climbed even faster to 34.3 billion, more than three times where they stood two years ago. Merged pull requests more than tripled to 1.3 billion over the same period, an average of 3.5 million a day. AI has helped us all build faster. With this volume, and more to be expected, we must keep accessibility top of mind so that the code that is being shipped is accessible to all. > As the home for all developers, we want every developer to feel welcome and to be able to contribute to the future of global software development using everything GitHub ha...

Infra & Chips.content: NVIDIA and Microsoft are extending their full-stack collaboration to help organizations build, customize and deploy intelligent applications — from next-generation infrastructure on Azure to industrial systems and Windows PCs. At Microsoft Ignite, the companies are expanding access to Azure virtual machines powered by NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 systems, as well as adding customer availability to NVIDIA open models and customization capabilities through Microsoft Foundry, and new options for running AI at the edge, where businesses generate and use their data. Microsoft is also using NVIDIA technologies to accelerate its own models and services, including NVIDIA Dynamo inference software for post-training and NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs for Bing search models. ## **NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 Running in Azure** NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 systems are running in Azure data centers, providing infrastructure designed for demanding reasoning, agentic applications, and large-scale model training and inference. Microsoft and NVIDIA are also collaborating to extend confidential computing to bare-metal and rack-scale AI infrastructure. The work will help protect sensitive models and data while they are being processed, supporting organizations that need to work with proprietary or regulated information. NVIDIA Confidential Computing and attestation help customers verify the computing environment before releasing sensitive models, data or keys. Infra & Chips.titleZh: Nvidia Vera Rubin NVL72 systems run in Azure data centers
Infra & Chips.content: In an official announcement at Microsoft Ignite, Nvidia stated that its Vera Rubin NVL72 systems are running inside Microsoft Azure data centers. The company reported that the cloud deployment provides infrastructure designed for large-scale model training, inference, and reasoning workloads as the two companies extend their accelerated computing collaboration. Nvidia said the companies are expanding access to Azure virtual machines powered by the Vera Rubin systems while extending confidential computing protections to bare-metal and rack-scale infrastructure. According to the announcement, the companies are also collaborating on data center power efficiency using Nvidia MaxLPS, and Microsoft AI is deploying Nvidia Dynamo software to coordinate reinforcement learning rollout inference for GPU fleets. Under the expanded partnership, Microsoft Foundry is adding customer access to Nvidia open models, including the Nemotron 3.5 Super model for research agents and the Lightning model for low-latency tasks, Nvidia stated. The announcement noted that EY adapted Nemotron models using Microsoft Foundry's Programmed Training, reporting a 55% accuracy improvement on its evaluation dataset alongside a fifteenfold cost reduction compared with proprietary frontier models. Beyond central data centers, Nvidia stated that Azure Local will support Nemotron 3.5 models and partner-provided Nvidia RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell graphics cards for on-premises deployments. For cloud computing users, the companies plan to release a public preview of Direct Stream for GPU-accelerated Windows 365 Cloud PCs in early 2027 following an initial limited preview, according to the announcement.

Infra & Chips.titleZh: Power-efficient inference chips let enterprises own AI hardware - SiliconANGLE
Infra & Chips.content: ### AI inference servers shrink to fit the air-cooled racks enterprises already run Power-efficient inference chips are becoming the entry price for enterprises that want to run AI on hardware they own. As AI shifts from building models to running them every day, costly graphics processing unit racks and the liquid cooling they demand keep many companies renting compute instead. That gap is opening room for challengers to the incumbent chipmakers. Axelera AI B.V. built its business at the edge with low-power chips and edge AI development tools, and it is now taking that technology into data center infrastructure, according to Manuel Botija (pictured), vice president and head of product at Axelera. “Enterprises cannot own their own infrastructure. They’re locked out because of the cost and the power,” Botija said. “We are enabling them now to own it. It’s not that we are helping the world save power or save money — which we are — but it’s that we are unlocking use cases that were simply not possible before.” Botija spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how power-efficient inference chips are heading for the data center and how enterprises locked out by the cost and power of GPU racks can own their own AI infrastructure instead of renting compute. *(* Disclosure below.)* ### Power-efficient inference chips head for the data center Axelera’s Europa chip has been shipping since September. Ahead of SC26, the company unveiled Titania, a third-generation architecture that scales the design up to a 400-watt chip. The resulting six-kilowatt server is built to perform like leading data center GPUs while fitting into the existing 20- to 30-kilowatt air-cooled racks of an ordinary enterprise data center, Botija explained. “Having a six-kilowatt server that can perform like a data centre GPU is a pretty big deal,” he said. “It basically means that they have some storage equipment, some networking equipment, some traditional CPU equipment, and next to all of that, they can also insert some AI inference hardware acceleration without needing to go and rebuild another server room or another data center.” For enterprises that would rather own their AI hardware than pay a recurring cloud bill, the barriers have been steep. A GPU rack costs at least $1 million, often far more, and usually requires liquid cooling, Botija noted. Axelera’s answer rests on digital in-memory computing, a technique that grew out of its founders’ research and gives the company’s power-efficient inference chips a performance-per-watt advantage. “Now you can own your own infrastructure,” Botija said. “You can amortize those investments and … reduce your opex, and therefore be more profitable as a company.” Here’s the complete video interview, part of SiliconANGLE’s and theCUBE’s coverage of SC26: *(* Disclosure: NYSE Wired sponsored this segment of theCUBE. Infra & Chips.titleZh: 800 VDC and NVIDIA DSX: the AI factory is changing. Europe's real test is delivery.
Infra & Chips.content: # 800 VDC and NVIDIA DSX: the AI factory is changing. Europe's real test is delivery. The 800 VDC architecture, the NVIDIA DSX reference architecture, and the new NVIDIA 800 VDC roadmap suggest a totally new approach to the implementation of AI infrastructure. In the case of Europe, the question goes beyond technology and is about access to the grid, investment decisions, and a capacity to realize the development opportunity. ## The next generation of AI infrastructure is taking shape Until now, a megawatt of power was a considerable amount in an entire data hall, but NVIDIA is now developing a system whereby a single rack can approach that level of consumption. The consequences for the mechanical and electrical systems are considerable, as well as for the economics of large-scale artificial intelligence. May 2025 saw the presentation of NVIDIA's roadmap for 800VDC, a significant deviation from the conventional data center electrical architecture. Eighteen months later, the transition is moving away from mere paper engineering. The components required are being developed, the reference architectures are becoming increasingly precise, and the first reported commercial deployments are emerging. The pace at which the market is changing has been illustrated by two recent developments. In March NVIDIA launched its DSX AI factory design, then in October it launched the expanded DSX platform and the DSX POD reference architecture. And then on 2 November, China's Envision announced what it described as the first commercial implementation of an integrated 800V power system in a large-scale AI data center. These developments, as individuals, are all technologically important. However, they are pointing to a much deeper change in the way AI infrastructure is going to be designed, built and operated. For years now, data centers have been built with one basic assumption: they provide a reliable power supply, a high-quality building, and enough computing equipment to deliver what the client has paid for. The coming generation of AI-based platforms are putting this assumption to the test. Everything, the computing equipment, power distribution, cooling, power storage, and even interfacing with the local power grid, has become increasingly integrated. As one who has spent much of my career at the intersection of technology, strategy, and data center design, I can tell you that this transition needs a lot more attention from both industry and investors. It is not only a question of increasing the power to the racks, which grow more and more demanding, but of reconsidering the conversion of power into useful work, the financing of the infrastructure, and the execution of projects in markets where the availability of energy is one of the most important restrictions on growth. ## Why 800 VDC is becoming an architectural necessity The rationale behind 800 VDC begins with a relatively simple engineering challenge: AI computing systems are consuming substantially more electricity within increasingly concentrated physical footprints. Traditional enterprise racks commonly operated at between 5 and 10 kW. High-density AI systems now exceed 100 kW, with future architectures targeting several hundred kilowatts per rack, and NVIDIA's Kyber roadmap extends that trajectory toward rack power requirements approaching 1 MW. When you get to that density, you are running up against the limitations of conventional distribution. Electric power is the product of voltage and current, and when you're dealing with relatively low voltage, you need a higher current. That means you need bigger wires, and more losses, and a greater demand on the wiring and electrical system. NVIDIA has highlighted the limitations of extending today's 54 VDC rack distribution architecture to megawatt-scale systems.
